subject: orthopaedics
title: Acute Compartment Syndrome

steps.tx: **Acute compartment syndrome** is an orthopaedic surgical emergency in which elevated interstitial tissue pressure within an unyielding, non-compliant osteofascial compartment exceeds capillary perfusion pressure. This microvascular collapse induces progressive cellular hypoxia, tissue ischaemia, and rapid neuromuscular necrosis. Common etiologies include closed and open tibial shaft fractures, forearm fractures, crush injuries, reperfusion following prolonged arterial occlusion, tight circumferential plaster casts, and pressurized intravenous fluid extravasation.
steps.say: Acute compartment syndrome is an orthopaedic emergency where rising tissue pressure inside an inflexible fascial space strangles capillary blood flow. Unless decompressed immediately, irreversible muscle and nerve necrosis follows within hours.

vis.alt: Diagram illustrating early fracture complications including acute compartment syndrome.
vis.caption: Early fracture complications: intracompartmental swelling, fascial confinement, and neurovascular ischaemia. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: **Passive muscle stretch** eliciting severe, deep, crescendo pain represents the earliest, most sensitive and reliable clinical physical sign of impending compartment syndrome. Before sensory deficits or skin changes appear, gentle passive stretching of muscles originating within the involved compartment produces agonizing pain. In the anterior compartment of the leg, passive plantarflexion of the ankle and toes stretches the tibialis anterior and extensor hallucis longus, reproducing intense ischemic pain.
steps.say: Pain out of proportion to the injury and agonizing pain on passive stretching of the compartment muscles is the earliest and most reliable sign. In the anterior leg, stretching the toes into plantarflexion reproduces intense pain.

left.title: Early Diagnostic Signs
points: Severe pain out of proportion to injury
Agonizing pain on passive muscle stretch

steps.tx: **Delta pressure** represents the difference between diastolic blood pressure and measured intracompartmental tissue pressure, providing the definitive physiological diagnostic threshold. A delta pressure of thirty millimetres of mercury or less indicates critical tissue hypoperfusion demanding emergent surgical fasciotomy. Relying on an arbitrary absolute compartment pressure of thirty millimetres of mercury alone can be misleading in hypotensive patients, making delta pressure calculation the safest clinical decision standard.
steps.say: Delta pressure is diastolic blood pressure minus compartment pressure. When delta pressure falls to thirty millimetres of mercury or less, capillary perfusion ceases, establishing an absolute indication for emergency fasciotomy.

vis.title: Compartmental Pressure Parameters and Thresholds
rows: Measure within 5 cm of fracture zone
Tissue ischaemia occurs at lower ICP

steps.tx: **Anterior tibial compartment** of the lower leg represents the most common anatomical site for acute compartment syndrome, particularly following high-energy closed tibial shaft fractures. Bounded by the rigid tibia medially, the fibula laterally, the interosseous membrane posteriorly, and the tough anterior crural fascia anteriorly, it tightly encloses the tibialis anterior, extensor digitorum longus, extensor hallucis longus, anterior tibial artery, and deep peroneal nerve.
steps.say: The anterior leg compartment is the most frequent site of compartment syndrome after tibial fractures. It is tightly boxed in by the tibia, fibula, and anterior fascia, housing the deep peroneal nerve and foot dorsiflexors.

vis.title: The Four Anatomical Compartments of the Leg
rows: Tibialis anterior, EHL, EDL, peroneus tertius
Deep peroneal nerve, anterior tibial artery
Tibial nerve, posterior tibial artery, peroneal artery

steps.tx: **Bedside cast bivalving** must be executed immediately upon the slightest clinical suspicion of developing compartment syndrome. Completely splitting all circumferential plaster or fibreglass cast materials down to the underlying skin, together with dividing all constricting cotton padding bandages, reduces intracompartmental tissue pressure by sixty to seventy percent. The affected limb must be maintained strictly at heart level: elevating the limb further reduces arterial perfusion pressure, accelerating ischemic necrosis.
steps.say: Immediately bivalve any tight cast down to bare skin, cutting through all cotton bandages. This relieves up to seventy percent of pressure. Keep the limb at heart level: never elevate it, as elevation reduces arterial inflow.

steps.tx: **Emergent surgical fasciotomy** represents the definitive therapeutic intervention when delta pressure falls to thirty millimetres of mercury or less, or clinical signs persist after cast release. Complete surgical unroofing of all affected fascial envelopes must be accomplished without delay. For the lower leg, a two-incision four-compartment fasciotomy is standard: an anterolateral incision releases the anterior and lateral compartments, while a posteromedial incision releases the superficial and deep posterior compartments.
steps.say: Emergent two-incision four-compartment fasciotomy is the definitive surgery. An anterolateral incision opens the anterior and lateral compartments, while a posteromedial incision decompresses the superficial and deep posterior spaces.

left.title: Anterolateral Incision
points: Placed midway between fibula and tibial crest

right.title: Posteromedial Incision
points: Placed 2 cm posterior to posterior tibial border
Detaches soleus bridge to release deep posterior

steps.tx: **Myonecrosis** begins within four to eight hours of sustained compartment ischaemia, progressing to complete, irreversible muscle death after eight hours. Peripheral sensory nerve conduction fails within thirty minutes of ischaemia, with permanent axonal injury solidifying after eight hours. Late delayed fasciotomy performed beyond twenty-four to thirty-six hours after onset carries severe risks: exposing dead necrotic muscle to atmospheric air invites overwhelming bacterial sepsis and life-threatening wound infections.
steps.say: Muscle begins dying within four to eight hours of complete ischemia, and damage is irreversible after eight hours. Fasciotomy delayed past twenty-four hours is dangerous because opening dead muscle invites overwhelming infection.

nodes.label: 8 Hours and Beyond

steps.tx: **Volkmann ischaemic contracture** is the catastrophic end-stage cicatricial sequela of untreated forearm compartment syndrome, classically following supracondylar humerus fractures in children. Ischemic infarction of the deep volar forearm flexors, predominantly flexor digitorum profundus and flexor pollicis longus, leads to extensive fibroblastic replacement and contracture. The clinical presentation is marked by fixed wrist flexion, compensatory hyperextension of metacarpophalangeal joints, and acute flexion of interphalangeal joints producing a claw-hand deformity.
steps.say: Volkmann ischemic contracture is the tragic late outcome of missed forearm compartment syndrome. The infarcted deep finger flexors turn into rigid scar tissue, producing a classic fixed claw-like hand deformity.

vis.title: Grading of Volkmann Ischaemic Contracture
rows: FDP, FPL, and superficial flexor digitorum
